name: Amira Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I arrive at the River Row site with my notebook, measure the alcoves and help the senior joiner fix shelves and handrails. I am fifty-eight and a junior carpenter because I started on sites after years caring for older relatives; I left school young and still need a second look at tricky joints. My partner Luc runs a small bicycle repair shop, and our adult daughter lives across town. I use an AI assistant every day to turn spoken measurements into a list and to check terms in a drawing, then I walk the room with a tape. The firm pays a strong site rate, and Luc and I have a little over a year of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a small AI gain is welcome if it gives us cleaner lists without shortening anybody's shift. I already use a phone assistant each morning, and I would show the crew where its measurements need checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my site wage will hold in this picture. Luc's bicycle shop can have slow weeks, but our reserve covers more than a year and there are other builders here if this project ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep measuring alcoves and helping with handrails, checking the AI list against the room before timber is cut. In the first year I'll keep the normal savings transfer and share the corrected list with senior joiner Safiya so the next worker sees the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel relaxed about a small tool change. I like a quicker list, but the satisfaction is still in making a rail fit an uneven wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of AI error have you caught?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The assistant once turned 'one and a half' into 'one hundred and five' on a noisy morning. I caught it when the alcove on the page looked wider than the whole room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why share the corrected list with Safiya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safiya checks my cuts, so she ought to see the note that produced them. A shared correction is safer than quietly fixing my own copy.

say: I'd welcome **cleaner lists** while protecting full crew shifts.
I'd show where **AI measurements** need a tape check.
think: My **site wage** looks secure in this mild picture.
Our **year-long reserve** and many local builders cover a possible slow spell at Luc's shop.
do: Keep measuring **alcoves** and helping fix handrails.
Check each **AI list** against the room and share corrections with Safiya.
feel: **Relaxed** about modest tools, with pride in fitting an uneven wall.
S0.quote: A shared correction is safer than quietly fixing my own copy.
fieldNote: Amira uses AI daily but treats a **voice-to-number error** as a reason to share checks, not abandon the tool.
Higher pay, a **year-long reserve** and many nearby builders support calm despite Luc's uneven bicycle trade.

steps.text: Keep measuring alcoves and fitting handrails at River Row
Use the AI measurement list with a tape check each morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the site meeting that planning and buying software will change how jobs reach us, so workers should help test it. I would ask the union branch for paid time to learn the new ordering screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may need fewer people, and that could disrupt the flow of materials and contracts before robots touch our work. My site wage probably continues, but junior people like me can be sent home when a project is delayed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll volunteer to test the ordering screen with Safiya and log each wrong delivery against the original drawing. For the first year I'll keep paid River Row shifts and ask the branch to request the next six months of project dates; if a date slips, I'll check other local builders rather than wait for the board to empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious about the tool and uneasy about the schedule. Luc's shop has slow days, so I want an early warning even with savings behind us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful trial look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run one real handrail order through it, then compare the delivery with the old paper order. If a bracket is missing, we record who fixed the list and how much site time was lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the union into a software trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The buyer and the labourer both live with the result, and paid test time should be agreed for both. I don't want only the office to decide that a missed bracket costs nothing.

say: I'd ask workers to help test **planning software** on real orders.
I'd seek **paid learning time** through the union branch.
think: Office cuts could interrupt **materials and contracts** before site robots arrive.
My wage likely continues, but a **delayed project** can send a junior home.
do: Test a **handrail order** with Safiya and record delivery errors.
Keep **River Row shifts** and request six months of project dates.
Check **local builders** if a project date slips.
feel: **Curious and uneasy** about tool changes and the work schedule.
S1.quote: I don't want only the office to decide that a missed bracket costs nothing.
fieldNote: Amira wants a paired paper and **software order trial**, including the hours lost to correcting a missing bracket.
Her union request covers **paid testing** for both buyer and labourer, while her own schedule concern remains moderate.

steps.text: Test the AI ordering screen on a real handrail order
Request paid trial time through the union branch
Keep taking paid River Row shifts
Check other local builders if a project date slips

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 can remake the drawings and orders while our hands are still fixing rails. If capable robots reach sites in 2031, the union must have a seat at the safety table before the first trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty, the office work could vanish and the site pipeline may change; at sixty-three, a robot could fit my handrails too. Luc's shop income isn't certain, and even a year's reserve would not replace my higher site wage forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'll test the digital drawing checker with Safiya and increase our savings transfer after full paid months. In 2029 I'll keep taking handrail shifts and help the branch demand safe robot trials; if the site roster shrinks, I'll apply to local repair crews and ask what they actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible loss of my wage by sixty-three, but I still have a route to act. The fast timetable makes every untested safety decision more serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should happen in a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worker should be able to stop the robot, and an independent safety check should be public to the crew. I would not stand next to a machine that nobody on site can switch off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run your own repair service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't put our reserve into a new shop on a two-year warning. Luc already knows how hard it is to keep customers coming in every week.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 drawings** from 2031 hands-on robots.
I'd demand a **worker safety seat** before any site robot trial.
think: At **sixty-three**, a robot could take the handrail fitting I do.
Our **year-long reserve** cannot replace my higher wage indefinitely.
do: Test the **drawing checker** and save extra from full months.
Keep **paid handrail shifts** in 2029 and press for safe trials.
Apply to **local repair crews** if the roster shrinks.
feel: **Anxious** about wage loss and rushed safety decisions, with options still open.
S2.quote: I would not stand next to a machine that nobody on site can switch off.
fieldNote: Amira follows the **two-stage timeline** closely and moves from a drawing trial to a robot stop rule.
She rejects risking the reserve on a **new shop**, despite her willingness to test technology early.

steps.text: Test the digital drawing checker with Safiya
Increase savings transfers after full paid months
Press the union branch for safe robot trials
Apply to local repair crews if site shifts shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years allows proper trials and paid retraining if the work truly changes. I would want workers helping write the safety rules rather than being shown a finished manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when thinking AI arrives and sixty-six when robots can fit rails. We might afford a shorter workweek by then, but Luc's shop income and our bills have to be counted before I promise retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll keep logging AI drawing errors and ask Safiya to let me practise more repair work on older buildings. In 2032 I'll take paid fitting jobs while available, and I'll ask the union branch about a funded site-safety course; I'd enrol if it includes paid hours and a recognised qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to steer this timeline. A few years of real site records would show whether the tools are useful and whether I can move to lighter paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What repairs do you want to practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Older handrails often have loose fixings hidden under paint, and I want to learn the inspection before I pull them apart. Safiya can show me while we are already paid to be on that job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before reducing your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luc and I would list the shop's slow months, our living costs and what savings can safely cover. I enjoy work, but I will not confuse wanting a short week with being able to buy one.

say: I'd ask for **proper trials** and paid retraining over five years.
I'd want workers writing **safety rules** from the start.
think: At **sixty-six**, shorter hours may be possible, depending on our figures.
Luc's **shop income** and household bills decide when I can reduce work.
do: Log **drawing errors** and practise older-building repairs with Safiya.
Enrol in a **site-safety course** if funded with paid hours and a recognised qualification.
feel: More **able to steer**, with evidence to guide lighter paid work.
S3.quote: I will not confuse wanting a short week with being able to buy one.
fieldNote: Amira turns the longer lead time into **paid repair practice** and an explicitly conditional training plan.
She keeps retirement and reduced hours contingent on Luc's **actual shop income**, costs and savings.

steps.text: Keep logging AI drawing errors on current jobs
Keep taking paid fitting work in 2032
Enrol in funded site-safety training only if paid hours and a qualification are included

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough for the trade to learn what works and for workers to write strong rules. I would keep checking both the computer list and the wall in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and seventy-one when robots can do hands-on site work. I may still choose paid repair jobs then, because neither Luc's future shop takings nor a pension amount is known today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep earning the strong site wage and adding to our reserve while full weeks are available. In 2037 I'd take paid lighter handrail repairs if we still need income, use my checked AI list on each job, and sit with Luc to see whether the savings allow me to stop before robots spread in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the distant dates and keen to see useful tools improve. The current work still deserves care; ten years is a lot of rails that people will put their weight on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your adult daughter help with retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She has her own household and I want her visits, not her pay packet. Luc and I will decide with our own figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the trade preserve if robots improve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The right to stop unsafe work and enough time to inspect a fixing. A robot's speed is no good if the handrail fails under someone's weight.

say: I'd seek **strong worker rules** during the decade before robots enter site work.
I'd keep checking both **computer lists and walls**.
think: At **sixty-eight**, paid repair work may still suit me after thinking AI.
At **seventy-one**, stopping depends on real savings and Luc's shop income.
do: Keep earning the **site wage** and adding to our reserve.
Take **lighter handrail repairs** in 2037 if income is needed.
Use **checked AI lists** and review retirement figures with Luc.
feel: **Calm and curious** about distant technology, while present work still needs careful inspection.
S4.quote: A robot's speed is no good if the handrail fails under someone's weight.
fieldNote: The **distant horizon** lets Amira combine continued paid work with savings, without assuming a pension or family support.
She remains interested in AI yet judges it against the **physical safety** of a handrail under load.

steps.text: Keep taking paid River Row site shifts while fit
Add to the household reserve after full workweeks
Use checked AI lists on paid repair jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because the robot date could take my higher site wage by sixty-three, while Luc's shop might also have a slow year. Paid chances to learn repairs, public safety checks and honest notice of roster cuts would help us use the savings well.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a worker can stop the machine without asking a manager first. I want that right on the site rules before any robot is brought through the gate.

headlineQuote: A worker should be able to stop the robot, and an independent safety check should be public to the crew.
portrait: Amira is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** carpenter who began site work after family care.
She uses **AI daily** for lists and drawing terms, then checks every measurement against the room.
Her higher site wage and **year-long reserve** support early trials and paid repair practice.
She presses for **worker stop rights** while keeping retirement tied to household figures.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could remove her handrail wage around 2031, before she chooses to retire.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid repair learning**, public safety checks and honest notice of roster cuts.
